title: Machine Learning Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Machine Learning lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Learn from examples
entries.summary: Machine learning uses examples to choose a rule or model. A model is a stored way to make predictions. A prediction is an estimate, not a known fact.
notes: Do not say that every learner reads at the same speed.

entries.name: Inputs and known answers
entries.summary: A feature is an input used for a prediction. A label is the known answer in a teaching example. Keep each input paired with the right answer.
notes: Shuffling inputs without shuffling their matching labels breaks the pairs.

entries.name: Regression predicts numbers
entries.summary: Regression is a task that predicts a number. Here we supply a doubling rule ourselves so the calculation is easy to inspect.
notes: A hand-written rule is not automatically a learned model.

entries.name: Classification chooses a group
entries.summary: Classification predicts a group label. For this toy example, a threshold is the number where our choice changes.
notes: A class label is a choice of group; it does not show how certain that choice is.

entries.name: Try the nearest example
entries.summary: A nearest-neighbour rule uses the closest stored example. Distance tells us how far two values are apart. Here distance is the size of their difference.

example.code:
examples = [(1, "small"), (3, "small"), (8, "large")]
query = 7
nearest = min(examples, key=lambda row: abs(row[0] - query))
print(nearest[1])

notes: One nearby example may be noisy or wrong; it is not enough evidence for a serious decision.

entries.name: Keep a test set aside
entries.summary: Training examples help choose a model. Test examples are kept aside to check it later. Keeping them separate helps reveal mistakes on unseen data.

example.code:
rows = [(1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6), (4, 8)]
train = rows[:3]
test = rows[3:]
print(len(train), len(test))

notes: Real splits must account for time and related records; a simple slice is not always fair.

entries.name: Compare with a baseline
entries.summary: A baseline is a simple prediction rule used for comparison. Always guessing the training average is one baseline for a number task.
notes: A more complex model should earn its complexity by passing useful checks.

entries.name: Measure a numeric mistake
entries.summary: Absolute error is the size of the difference between an answer and a prediction. It drops the minus sign so the size is always nonnegative.

example.code:
answers = [4, 8]
predictions = [5, 6]
errors = [abs(a - p) for a, p in zip(answers, predictions)]
print(errors, sum(errors) / len(errors))

notes: Keep the units: an error of 1.5 minutes is different from 1.5 hours.

entries.name: Accuracy needs context
entries.summary: Accuracy is the share of group guesses that are correct. It can hide poor performance on a rare group.

example.code:
answers = ["dry", "dry", "dry", "rain"]
predictions = ["dry"] * 4
correct = sum(a == p for a, p in zip(answers, predictions))
print(correct / len(answers))

notes: A high overall score can hide failure on the group that matters most.

entries.name: Memorising is not generalising
entries.summary: Overfitting happens when a model follows training details too closely and does poorly on new examples. Generalising means working on useful new cases.
notes: Do not choose a model only by its training score.

entries.name: Group without answer labels
entries.summary: Clustering groups similar inputs without known class labels. Here we check distance to two fixed centres; a real clustering method can learn its centres.

example.code:
centres = [2, 8]
point = 7
distances = [abs(point - centre) for centre in centres]
print(distances.index(min(distances)))

notes: A discovered group does not explain why its members are alike.

entries.name: Write an honest model report
entries.summary: A useful model report explains the task, data, checks and limits. Readers need enough detail to know where the result may fail.

example.code:
Task: estimate reading minutes
Data: fictional page-and-time pairs
Check: compare held-out errors with a simple baseline
Limit: too little data for real learners
Decision: keep this as a classroom demonstration

notes: Keep private information out of practice data and include a human review for important decisions.
